parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
In the following list, underline all particles that are leptons.

antineutrino             positron             proton             quark

markscheme_points.text: proton and positron both underlined (and no others);

hints: Hint 1: Think about the two families of fundamental matter particles - quarks and leptons - and remember that protons are made of quarks, so they cannot be leptons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember what a lepton is**
Leptons are fundamental (not made of anything smaller) particles that do not feel the strong force. The lepton family includes electrons, muons, taus, neutrinos and all their antiparticles, including positrons and antineutrinos.

Step 2: **Sort the list**
Antineutrino is a lepton, positron (the antiparticle of the electron) is a lepton. Proton is a hadron (a baryon made of three quarks) so it is not a lepton. Quark is fundamental but belongs to the quark family, not the lepton family.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A stationary nucleus of magnesium-27, $^{27}_{12}\text{Mg}$, decays by emitting a $\beta^-$ particle and $\gamma$ radiation. An incomplete equation to represent this decay is

$$^{27}_{12}\text{Mg} \rightarrow X + \beta^- + \gamma.$$
parts.text: State the nucleon number and the proton number of nucleus X.
hints: Hint 1: Look at what the $\beta^-$ particle and $\gamma$ photon contribute to the top (nucleon) and bottom (proton) numbers in the decay equation.
Hint 2: Use conservation - the total top numbers and total bottom numbers must balance on both sides to find X.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply conservation of nucleon number**
In any nuclear decay the total nucleon number $A$ (top number) is conserved. A $\beta^-$ particle has $A = 0$ and $\gamma$ has $A = 0$, so they do not change the nucleon count. Therefore $$A_X = 27$$

Step 2: **Apply conservation of proton number / charge**
The total proton number $Z$ (bottom number, charge) is also conserved. A $\beta^-$ particle is an electron with $Z = -1$ and $\gamma$ has $Z = 0$. So $$12 = Z_X + (-1)$$ which gives $$Z_X = 12 + 1 = 13$$ This is the $\beta^-$ decay rule: a neutron changes to a proton, so $Z$ increases by 1 while $A$ stays the same.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the name of the interaction that gives rise to this decay.
hints: Hint 1: Recall which of the four fundamental forces is responsible for changing quark flavour and allowing neutrons to turn into protons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link beta decay to the fundamental forces**
Alpha decay and fission are governed by the strong force breaking apart, and gamma emission is electromagnetic. Only $\beta$ decay changes a neutron into a proton (a down quark into an up quark). That flavour change is always caused by the weak interaction.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: State **two** possible reasons why the sum of the kinetic energy of the $\beta^-$ particle and the energy of the $\gamma$ radiation is less than the total energy released during the decay of the magnesium nucleus.

markscheme_points.text: electron neutrino / \bar{\nu}_{(e)} is produced (and this carries away);

hints: Hint 1: Think about the full $\beta^-$ decay equation at quark and nucleon level - an extra very hard to detect lepton is always emitted alongside the $\beta^-$ particle but is missing from the simplified equation given.
Hint 2: Think about where the total released energy (from mass loss) must go if it is shared between more than just the $\beta^-$ particle and the $\gamma$ photon.
parts.proper_answer: 1. An (electron) antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_e$ is also produced in the decay. 2. This antineutrino carries away part of the released energy (as kinetic energy).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the missing particle**
The complete $\beta^-$ decay is $$n \rightarrow p + \beta^- + \bar{\nu}_e$$ A stationary magnesium nucleus decays, so the full nuclear equation should include an electron antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_e$. It was left out of the incomplete equation.

Step 2: **Explain the missing energy**
Total energy released comes from the loss of mass (mass-energy is conserved). This energy is shared as kinetic energy and photon energy between all products. Because the antineutrino escapes undetected and carries away momentum and energy, the measured sum of only the $\beta^-$ kinetic energy plus the $\gamma$ energy is less than the total. This sharing is also why $\beta^-$ particles have a continuous range of energies.
